description: The 39 facets of the facet-duplicate judging study (fixtures/linear_algebra at 7b44c9b0) and its labels: the 12 pairs both judges call merge-worthy and the pairs both call related_distinct at cosine >= 0.5. Source: docs/reviews/facet-duplicate-judging-2026-10-12.md.

facets.claim: A collection is linearly dependent when a vector is redundant because it lies in the span of the others; a basis is a linearly independent collection that spans the entire vector space.
preconditions: A collection of vectors in a vector space is specified.
Span is understood.
applicability: Determining whether a collection qualifies as a basis.
positive_examples: A spanning collection in which no vector lies in the span of the others.
negative_examples: A spanning collection containing a vector already generated by the remaining vectors.
An independent collection that does not span the whole space.
non_goals: Spanning alone and independence alone are each insufficient for being a basis.
error_signatures: Assuming every added vector contributes a new direction.
Calling any spanning collection a basis without checking independence.
instructional_repairs: Test whether removing any vector leaves the span unchanged.
Check spanning and linear independence as separate requirements.

facets.claim: A complex number has the form a + bi with a,b real, and the set of all such numbers is denoted C.
preconditions: The learner can recognize real numbers and ordered pairs of real values.
applicability: Representing and interpreting complex numbers.
non_goals: This definition alone does not specify complex addition or multiplication.
error_signatures: Treating a and b as non-real coefficients without changing the number system.
Omitting the imaginary unit from the second component.
instructional_repairs: Rewrite the number explicitly as a + bi and identify both real coefficients.

facets.claim: A field is a set containing distinct elements 0 and 1 with addition and multiplication satisfying the field properties; examples include the rational numbers with their usual operations and the two-element field {0, 1} in which 1 + 1 = 0.
applicability: Identifying the scalar systems allowed in abstract linear algebra.
positive_examples: The rational numbers with usual arithmetic.
The two-element field with 1 + 1 = 0.
negative_examples: Rejecting a structure merely because its addition differs from familiar real-number arithmetic.
non_goals: This facet does not reconstruct field axioms omitted from the extracted unit.
error_signatures: Assuming every field must satisfy 1 + 1 ≠ 0.
instructional_repairs: Judge a candidate field by its stated operations and field properties, not by familiarity alone.

facets.claim: A linear combination is a sum of scalar multiples of given vectors, and the span of a collection is the set of all linear combinations obtainable as every coefficient varies over the scalar field.
preconditions: A collection of vectors and its scalar field are specified.
applicability: Describing reachable vectors and testing whether a collection spans a space.
positive_examples: Two non-collinear vectors in three-dimensional space span a plane through the origin.
Two non-aligned vectors in the plane span the plane.
negative_examples: A finite sample of linear combinations mistaken for the full span.
non_goals: A single displayed linear combination is not itself the span.
error_signatures: Restricting coefficients to only positive or sampled values.
Claiming that two non-collinear vectors span all of three-dimensional space.
instructional_repairs: Let every coefficient vary over the full scalar field.
Distinguish one generated vector from the set of all generated vectors.

facets.claim: A list of length n is a finite ordered collection of elements, where n is a nonnegative integer; the length-zero case is the empty list.
preconditions: n is a nonnegative integer.
applicability: Interpreting tuples and coordinate lists.
Determining whether an ordered object qualifies as a list.
positive_examples: (x,y) is a list of length two.
() is a list of length zero.
negative_examples: An infinitely long sequence-like object is not a list under this definition.
non_goals: This definition does not include infinite sequences.
error_signatures: Treating an infinite sequence as a finite list.
Assuming every list contains at least one entry.
instructional_repairs: Verify that the proposed length is a finite nonnegative integer.
Include the empty list when considering the n=0 boundary case.

facets.claim: A real number a is identified with a + 0i, while i denotes 0 + 1i and satisfies i^2 = -1.
preconditions: The learner can read a complex number in a + bi form.
applicability: Embedding real numbers into the complex numbers.
Interpreting and simplifying expressions involving i.
negative_examples: Every complex number is real.
non_goals: The identification of real numbers inside the complex numbers does not make every complex number real.
error_signatures: Concluding that all complex numbers are real.
Replacing i^2 with 1 or leaving it unreduced during basic arithmetic.
instructional_repairs: Check the imaginary coefficient: a complex number is real exactly when that coefficient is zero.
Replace i·i with -1 before combining real terms.

facets.claim: A vector space is a set equipped with addition and scalar multiplication whose operations satisfy the vector-space axioms; its elements are called vectors or points and need not be geometric arrows.
preconditions: A set and candidate addition and scalar multiplication operations are specified.
applicability: Recognizing abstract and concrete vector spaces.
positive_examples: The one-element space {0}.
Spaces of scalar sequences.
Spaces of scalar-valued functions with pointwise operations.
negative_examples: A set with operations that fail one or more vector-space axioms.
non_goals: This claim does not assert that every set or every pair of operations forms a vector space.
Vectors are not restricted to arrows or finite coordinate lists.
error_signatures: Rejecting functions as vectors solely because they are not geometric arrows.
Calling a set a vector space without specifying and checking its operations.
instructional_repairs: Identify the elements, addition, and scalar multiplication before applying the axiom checklist.
Separate the abstract vector-space structure from any particular representation of its elements.

facets.claim: A vector space is a set with addition and scalar multiplication satisfying commutativity of addition, associativity of vector addition and scalar multiplication, existence of an additive identity and additive inverses, the scalar identity law, and distributivity over vector and scalar addition.
preconditions: A set has specified addition and scalar multiplication operations.
The scalars belong to the relevant scalar system.
applicability: Recognizing or verifying abstract vector-space structure.
positive_examples: Check each axiom for all relevant vectors and scalars.
negative_examples: Concluding that a set is a vector space after checking only closure or commutativity.
non_goals: The definition does not require a norm, inner product, basis, dimension, or geometric realization.
error_signatures: Omitting one distributive law.
Confusing the scalar identity 1 with the additive identity 0.
Checking the axioms only for selected examples rather than universally.
instructional_repairs: Group the checks into addition laws, scalar-action laws, identity and inverse laws, and the two distributive laws.

facets.claim: A vector space is a set with operations of addition and scalar multiplication that satisfy algebraic properties; coordinate descriptions of the plane motivate this abstraction.
preconditions: A set and two proposed operations are under consideration.
The learner is familiar with sets and elementary arithmetic operations.
applicability: Introductory orientation before studying the formal vector-space axioms.
positive_examples: A coordinate description of a plane as motivation for a vector space.
non_goals: This introductory facet does not enumerate the formal vector-space axioms.
It does not establish that an arbitrary set with two operations is a vector space.
error_signatures: Calling any set a vector space without checking required algebraic properties.
instructional_repairs: Treat the statement as an introductory characterization and defer membership judgments until the formal axioms are available.

facets.claim: A vector space is called real or complex according to whether its scalar field is the real numbers or the complex numbers.
preconditions: The scalar field of the vector space is specified.
applicability: Distinguishing real and complex vector spaces.
positive_examples: A space over real scalars is a real vector space.
A space over complex scalars is a complex vector space.
non_goals: The classification does not change the underlying vector-space axiom pattern.
error_signatures: Classifying a vector space without identifying its scalar field.
instructional_repairs: Name the scalar field explicitly whenever the distinction matters.

facets.claim: Add complex numbers componentwise: (a + bi) + (c + di) = (a + c) + (b + d)i.
preconditions: Both addends are written in a + bi form.
Their coefficients are real numbers.
applicability: Adding two complex numbers in standard form.
negative_examples: (a + bi) + (c + di) = (a + b) + (c + d)i
non_goals: This rule does not define complex multiplication.
error_signatures: Combining a real component with an imaginary coefficient.
Dropping the imaginary unit from the result.
instructional_repairs: Align the real components and the coefficients of i as two separate columns before adding.

facets.claim: Addition assigns an element of the set to each ordered pair of its elements, while scalar multiplication assigns an element of the set to each scalar-element pair.
preconditions: A set of prospective vectors is specified.
A scalar domain is specified for scalar multiplication.
applicability: Specifying the operations of a candidate vector space.
positive_examples: Componentwise operations on scalar sequences.
Pointwise operations on scalar-valued functions.
negative_examples: An operation whose output can leave the proposed vector set.
non_goals: Closure of the operations alone does not establish all vector-space axioms.
error_signatures: Treating vector addition as an operation that may return an object outside the set.
Confusing scalar multiplication with multiplication of two vectors.
instructional_repairs: State each operation's input types and output set explicitly.
Check the axioms only after the operations are well-defined.

facets.claim: An addition on a set assigns an element of the set to each ordered pair of its elements, while scalar multiplication assigns an element of the set to each scalar-vector pair.
preconditions: A candidate set of vectors and a scalar domain are given.
applicability: Reading the data required before vector-space axioms can be tested.
positive_examples: Addition takes two vectors; scalar multiplication takes one scalar and one vector.
negative_examples: Treating scalar multiplication as an operation on two vectors.
non_goals: These operation contracts alone do not imply the vector-space axioms.
error_signatures: Ignoring closure in the set.
Confusing a scalar-vector input with a vector-vector input.
instructional_repairs: Write the type of each input and output before applying an operation.

facets.claim: An element of a vector space may be called a vector or a point; this terminology does not require the space to have a physical geometric realization.
preconditions: An element belongs to a vector space.
applicability: Reading abstract vector-space language.
positive_examples: Call a function, polynomial, or coordinate tuple a vector when it is an element of a vector space.
negative_examples: Assuming every vector must be a visible arrow in two or three dimensions.
non_goals: This does not supply a geometric model for every vector space.
error_signatures: Restricting the word vector to arrows.
Inferring physical coordinates from the word point.
instructional_repairs: Use membership in the vector space, rather than visual appearance, to identify vectors.

facets.claim: Complex addition and multiplication obey commutativity and associativity; 0 and 1 are their respective identities; every complex number has a unique additive inverse; every nonzero complex number has a unique multiplicative inverse; and multiplication distributes over addition.
preconditions: Complex addition and multiplication have been defined.
applicability: Simplifying complex expressions.
Justifying algebraic transformations over complex numbers.
Preparing to interpret complex numbers as scalars in vector spaces.
positive_examples: α + β = β + α
(αβ)λ = α(βλ)
λ(α + β) = λα + λβ
negative_examples: Claiming that zero has a multiplicative inverse.
non_goals: The proposition does not claim that arbitrary operations in arbitrary systems are commutative.
error_signatures: Omitting the nonzero restriction for multiplicative inverses.
Confusing a change of order with a change of grouping.
instructional_repairs: Name the law used at each transformation and check its hypotheses, especially the nonzero condition for inversion.

facets.claim: Coordinates are scalar coefficients relative to an ordered basis, so changing the basis can change a vector's coordinate list without changing the underlying vector or vector space.
preconditions: An ordered basis has been chosen.
A vector is expressed as a linear combination of the basis vectors.
applicability: Interpreting numerical vector coordinates and comparing coordinate systems.
positive_examples: In the standard plane basis, (3,-2) means three times the first basis vector plus negative two times the second.
negative_examples: Treating a coordinate pair as having an absolute geometric meaning without a basis.
non_goals: This facet does not supply a change-of-basis algorithm.
error_signatures: Identifying a vector with one particular coordinate list.
Using coordinates without specifying or assuming their ordered basis.
instructional_repairs: State the ordered basis before interpreting coordinates.
Separate the underlying vector from its basis-dependent description.

facets.claim: For a fixed positive integer n, F^n is the set of all length-n lists (x_1,...,x_n) whose entries belong to F.
preconditions: n is a positive integer.
F denotes R or C.
applicability: Recognizing or constructing elements of a coordinate space.
Specializing the notation to examples such as C^4.
positive_examples: C^4 consists of four-entry lists of complex numbers.
negative_examples: A list with a number of entries different from n is not an element of F^n.
non_goals: The definition does not require a physical visualization of the space.
error_signatures: Constructing an element with fewer or more than n coordinates.
Mixing coordinate entries from incompatible scalar systems.
instructional_repairs: Count the entries and verify that every entry belongs to the same chosen F.

facets.claim: For all x,y in F^n, coordinatewise addition is commutative: x+y=y+x.
preconditions: x and y belong to the same F^n.
Addition in F^n is coordinatewise.
Scalar addition in F is commutative.
applicability: Reordering two addends in F^n.
Understanding how scalar laws induce coordinate-space laws.
positive_examples: x+y=y+x for x,y in F^n.
non_goals: This does not establish commutativity for arbitrary operations.
error_signatures: Using vector commutativity as its own justification during the proof.
instructional_repairs: At the coordinate-reversal step, cite commutativity of scalar addition in F.

facets.claim: For functions with a common domain and scalar-valued outputs, vector addition and scalar multiplication are defined pointwise by adding function values or scaling each function value at every input.
preconditions: The functions share a domain.
Their outputs lie in the relevant scalar field.
applicability: Treating collections of scalar-valued functions as candidate vector spaces.
positive_examples: A scalar multiple evaluated at x equals the scalar times f(x).
negative_examples: Function composition used in place of vector addition.
Multiplication of two functions used in place of scalar multiplication.
non_goals: Pointwise vector-space operations do not define function composition.
error_signatures: Adding functions by adding their inputs.
Scaling only selected outputs.
Rejecting functions as vectors because they lack a finite coordinate-list appearance.
instructional_repairs: Choose an arbitrary input x and define the new function through its value at x.
Check closure and each axiom pointwise.

facets.claim: For x and y in F^n, coordinatewise addition is commutative: x + y = y + x; a coordinate proof applies scalar commutativity separately in every coordinate.
preconditions: x and y belong to F^n.
Vector addition in F^n is defined coordinatewise.
Addition in F is commutative.
applicability: Proving commutativity of addition in a coordinate space.
positive_examples: Expand x and y into coordinate lists, reverse the scalar addends in each coordinate, and recognize y + x.
non_goals: This does not prove commutativity for arbitrary operations called addition.
error_signatures: Treating vector commutativity as already established instead of invoking scalar commutativity.
Reordering coordinates rather than reversing the two addends within each coordinate.
instructional_repairs: Label the coordinatewise-definition step and the scalar-commutativity step separately.

facets.claim: For x = (x_1, ..., x_n), compute the additive inverse by negating every coordinate: -x = (-x_1, ..., -x_n), which satisfies x + (-x) = 0.
preconditions: x is given as a coordinate vector.
applicability: Computing additive inverses in coordinate spaces.
positive_examples: Negate each coordinate without changing coordinate order or vector length.
non_goals: This procedure does not define scalar multiplication or a dot product.
error_signatures: Negating only some coordinates.
Changing the number or order of coordinates.
instructional_repairs: Match each output coordinate -x_i to the corresponding input coordinate x_i.

facets.claim: If x=(x_1,...,x_n) belongs to F^n, then x_k is the kth coordinate of x for each index k from 1 through n.
preconditions: x belongs to F^n.
applicability: Reading indexed vector notation.
Aligning coordinates for componentwise operations.
positive_examples: In (x_1,x_2,x_3), x_2 is the second coordinate.
negative_examples: Calling x_k a coordinate when k lies outside 1,...,n.
non_goals: Explicit coordinates need not be introduced when a coordinate-free argument is available.
error_signatures: Changing coordinate order.
Confusing the vector x with one scalar coordinate x_k.
instructional_repairs: Track both the ambient vector and the coordinate index.
Use subscripted notation only when coordinates are needed.

facets.claim: In F^n, the zero vector is the length-n list (0, ..., 0). Because the symbol 0 is overloaded, its type must be inferred from the surrounding expression; in x + 0 = x with x in F^n, it denotes the zero vector.
preconditions: The ambient coordinate space and the operand types are known.
applicability: Expressions using 0 in both a scalar field and a coordinate space.
positive_examples: Interpret 0 in x + 0 = x as the zero vector when x belongs to F^n.
negative_examples: Interpreting the second operand of x + 0 as scalar zero when vector-scalar addition has not been defined.
non_goals: This does not identify scalar zero and the zero vector as the same kind of object.
error_signatures: Assuming every occurrence of 0 is a scalar.
Ignoring the domain of the addition operation.
instructional_repairs: Identify the type of each neighboring term and select the zero object belonging to the required domain.

facets.claim: In two dimensions, a coordinate-space element can be viewed as a point or as an arrow from the origin; translating an arrow parallel to itself without changing its length or direction preserves the vector represented.
preconditions: A two-dimensional geometric interpretation is being used.
applicability: Building geometric intuition for two-dimensional vectors.
positive_examples: Move an arrow parallel to itself before using it in a tip-to-tail construction.
negative_examples: Treating the moved arrow as a different vector solely because its initial point changed.
non_goals: The picture is not the formal definition of vectors in every dimension.
error_signatures: Equating a vector with one fixed arrow location.
Replacing algebraic definitions with physical geometry.
instructional_repairs: Separate the abstract vector from a particular arrow used to depict it.

facets.claim: In two dimensions, multiplication by a positive scalar preserves direction and scales length by that scalar, while multiplication by a negative scalar reverses direction and scales length by the scalar's absolute value.
preconditions: The vector is interpreted geometrically in two dimensions.
The sign of the scalar is known.
applicability: Interpreting scalar multiplication geometrically.
positive_examples: A positive factor stretches or shrinks without reversing direction.
A negative factor reverses direction and scales length by its magnitude.
negative_examples: Applying the positive-scalar direction rule to a negative scalar.
non_goals: This geometric rule is not a replacement for the coordinate definition.
error_signatures: Using a negative length.
Failing to reverse direction for a negative scalar.
instructional_repairs: Handle sign and magnitude separately: sign determines direction; absolute value determines length scale.

facets.claim: Many linear-algebra definitions and proofs extend to arbitrary fields, but generalization requires checking the hypotheses: inner-product results and results requiring conditions such as 1 + 1 ≠ 0 are explicit exceptions in the source's discussion.
preconditions: A theorem or definition is being transferred from a standard scalar field to another field.
applicability: Assessing whether a linear-algebra result remains valid over a different field.
positive_examples: Check whether a result uses inner-product structure or excludes fields with 1 + 1 = 0.
negative_examples: Assuming every result automatically holds over every field.
non_goals: This is not an unconditional theorem-transfer rule.
error_signatures: Dropping a field-characteristic condition.
Ignoring the stated inner-product exception.
instructional_repairs: List the theorem's field-dependent hypotheses before changing its scalar field.

facets.claim: Multiply complex numbers by distributing, replacing i^2 with -1, combining real and imaginary terms separately, and writing the result in a + bi form; equivalently, (a + bi)(c + di) = (ac - bd) + (ad + bc)i.
preconditions: Both factors are written in a + bi form.
The distributive property and i^2 = -1 are available.
applicability: Multiplying two complex numbers in standard form.
negative_examples: Treating i^2 as 1.
Combining real and imaginary terms as like terms.
non_goals: The closed formula need not be memorized independently of its derivation.
error_signatures: Leaving i^2 unreduced.
Using ac + bd for the real component.
Failing to distribute one term across the opposite factor.
instructional_repairs: Expand as an ordinary binomial product, mark the i^2 term, replace it with -1, and then collect the two component types.

facets.claim: Scalar calculations over R or C use commutative and associative addition and multiplication, additive and multiplicative identities, additive inverses, nonzero multiplicative inverses, and distributivity of multiplication over addition.
preconditions: The operands are scalars in the same choice of F.
A multiplicative inverse or division is used only for a nonzero scalar.
applicability: Justifying coordinatewise vector calculations.
Rewriting scalar expressions within a coordinate proof.
positive_examples: a+b=b+a for scalars a,b.
A nonzero complex scalar has a unique multiplicative inverse.
negative_examples: Dividing by the scalar zero.
non_goals: This facet does not assert these laws for arbitrary operations or arbitrary algebraic systems.
error_signatures: Using a multiplicative inverse without checking that the scalar is nonzero.
Invoking a vector property to justify a scalar-coordinate equality.
instructional_repairs: State the relevant scalar law at the coordinate where it is applied.
Check the nonzero condition before using division or a multiplicative inverse.

facets.claim: Scalar multiplication takes a scalar λ and a coordinate vector and returns the vector obtained by multiplying every coordinate by λ: λ(x_1, ..., x_n) = (λx_1, ..., λx_n).
preconditions: λ is a scalar.
The vector is given in coordinate form.
applicability: Computing scalar multiples of coordinate vectors.
positive_examples: Apply λ to every coordinate, including zero and negative coordinates.
negative_examples: Multiplying corresponding coordinates of two vectors.
Returning a scalar as though the operation were a dot product.
non_goals: This is not coordinatewise multiplication of two vectors and is not the dot product.
error_signatures: Using two vector operands.
Multiplying only one coordinate.
Returning a scalar instead of a vector.
instructional_repairs: Track the input-output types: scalar and vector in, vector out.

facets.claim: The set of infinite scalar sequences becomes a vector space when addition and scalar multiplication are defined componentwise; its additive identity is the all-zero sequence.
preconditions: All sequence entries belong to the same scalar field.
Corresponding coordinates are added and every coordinate is scaled by the given scalar.
applicability: Understanding and verifying sequence spaces as vector spaces.
positive_examples: Adding corresponding entries of two sequences.
Multiplying every entry of a sequence by one scalar.
negative_examples: Combining coordinates by inconsistent position-dependent rules without verifying the axioms.
non_goals: This facet does not assert that every subset of the sequence space is a vector space.
error_signatures: Using a single scalar operation on only one coordinate.
Identifying the additive identity as scalar 0 rather than the all-zero sequence.
instructional_repairs: Write the operation at an arbitrary coordinate and verify each axiom there.
Identify vector-space elements and scalars as different kinds of objects.

facets.claim: The zero vector in F^n is the length-n list 0=(0,...,0), whose entries are scalar zeros; it is the additive identity for coordinatewise addition.
preconditions: The ambient space is F^n.
applicability: Identifying the additive identity in a coordinate space.
Writing the zero vector in coordinates.
positive_examples: In F^3, the zero vector is (0,0,0).
negative_examples: A list containing a nonzero coordinate is not the zero vector.
non_goals: The vector zero and scalar zero are not the same type of object.
error_signatures: Using a zero list of the wrong length.
Treating the vector zero as a scalar.
instructional_repairs: Match the number of zero coordinates to n.
Distinguish the whole list from each scalar entry.

facets.claim: Throughout this setting, F denotes either R or C, and an element of F is called a scalar.
applicability: Reading field-independent notation in the chapter.
Identifying the type of coordinate entries.
positive_examples: A complex number is a scalar when F=C.
A real number is a scalar when F=R.
non_goals: This notation does not make F an arbitrary field in the cited source.
error_signatures: Treating F as a single unspecified numerical set unrelated to R or C.
instructional_repairs: Substitute R or C for F and check that every scalar belongs to the chosen set.

facets.claim: To add two elements of F^n, align equal coordinate indices, add each scalar pair x_k and y_k in F, and return the length-n list (x_1+y_1,...,x_n+y_n).
preconditions: Both operands belong to the same F^n.
Scalar addition is defined in F.
applicability: Computing sums of coordinate vectors.
Expanding vector addition in a coordinate proof.
negative_examples: Pairing x_1 with y_2.
Returning a list of a different length.
non_goals: This procedure does not define scalar multiplication.
error_signatures: Adding coordinates with different indices.
Omitting, reordering, or duplicating a coordinate.
instructional_repairs: Label corresponding positions before adding.
Check that the output retains exactly n entries in the original order.

facets.claim: To construct a vector sum geometrically in two dimensions, translate the second arrow so its initial point meets the first arrow's endpoint, then draw the sum from the first arrow's initial point to the translated arrow's endpoint.
preconditions: Both vectors are represented as arrows in two dimensions.
Parallel translation preserves the represented vector.
applicability: Geometric interpretation of two-dimensional vector addition.
positive_examples: Use an unchanged translated copy of the second vector in a tip-to-tail construction.
negative_examples: Changing the second arrow's length or direction during translation.
Drawing the resultant between the wrong endpoints.
non_goals: This is not the general computational method for spaces that cannot be visualized.
error_signatures: Joining the wrong endpoints.
Rotating or rescaling the translated arrow.
instructional_repairs: Mark the first tail, shared tip-tail junction, and final endpoint before drawing the resultant.

facets.claim: To prove a universal identity about complex multiplication from its definition, represent arbitrary operands as a + bi and c + di, expand both sides, use real-number laws to match their real and imaginary components, and conclude equality.
preconditions: The operands are arbitrary complex numbers.
The complex multiplication rule is available.
The relevant real-number laws are available.
applicability: Definition-based proofs of foundational complex-arithmetic identities.
The worked case of commutativity of complex multiplication.
positive_examples: Expanding αβ and βα and matching components to prove αβ = βα.
negative_examples: Checking a single numerical example and claiming a universal proof.
non_goals: This procedure does not make every complex-arithmetic proof a component expansion.
The worked argument directly proves commutativity, not all listed laws at once.
error_signatures: Using particular numbers when the claim is universal.
Asserting equality without matching both the real and imaginary components.
Invoking complex commutativity inside a proof intended to establish that same property.
instructional_repairs: Begin with arbitrary real coefficients, expand each side independently from the definition, and cite only previously available real-number laws.

facets.claim: To prove a vector identity in F^n by coordinates, represent the vectors as coordinate lists, expand the vector operations by definition, apply the appropriate scalar fact at every coordinate, and recognize the resulting list as the target vector expression.
preconditions: The vectors belong to F^n.
The relevant vector operations have coordinate definitions.
The required scalar property is available.
applicability: Proving commutativity of addition in F^n.
Other vector identities whose operations are defined coordinatewise.
positive_examples: Expand x+y, commute every scalar sum, and reassemble the result as y+x.
negative_examples: Citing the vector theorem being proved to justify the scalar-coordinate step.
non_goals: Coordinates need not be introduced when a simpler coordinate-free proof is available.
error_signatures: Skipping the definition-expansion step.
Applying a scalar law to whole vectors without justification.
Failing to reassemble the coordinate list as the target vector expression.
instructional_repairs: Label each equality by either a vector-operation definition or a scalar property.
Verify that every coordinate undergoes the same justified transformation.

facets.claim: Two lists are equal exactly when they have the same length and equal entries in the same positions; unlike sets, lists preserve order and repetitions.
preconditions: Both compared objects are lists.
applicability: Comparing tuples or coordinate lists.
Distinguishing list equality from set equality.
negative_examples: (3,5) does not equal (5,3).
(4,4) does not equal (4,4,4).
non_goals: This is not a criterion for equality of sets.
error_signatures: Ignoring order when comparing lists.
Discarding repeated entries.
Failing to compare list lengths.
instructional_repairs: Compare lengths first, then compare entries at each matching position.
Do not apply set-style equality rules to parenthesized lists.

facets.claim: Vector addition must be commutative and associative, possess an additive identity and additive inverses, while scalar multiplication must be associative, respect scalar 1, and satisfy both distributive laws.
preconditions: Addition and scalar multiplication are defined on the candidate set.
applicability: Verifying whether specified operations make a set into a vector space.
positive_examples: Checking componentwise sequence operations coordinate by coordinate.
negative_examples: Verifying only closure or only some of the listed laws.
non_goals: The checklist does not prescribe what the vectors must look like.
error_signatures: Omitting one distributive law.
Confusing the scalar identity 1 with the additive identity vector 0.
Assuming commutativity of scalar multiplication with vectors is an axiom.
instructional_repairs: Organize verification by the complete axiom families: addition, identity and inverse, scalar identity and associativity, and distributivity.
Keep scalar operations distinct from vector operations.

facets.claim: When the symbol 0 is overloaded, its surrounding operation and ambient types determine whether it denotes scalar zero or the zero vector; in x+0 with x in F^n, it denotes the zero vector because vector addition takes two elements of F^n.
preconditions: The symbol 0 occurs in a typed mathematical expression.
The domains of the surrounding operations are known.
applicability: Interpreting x+0=x in F^n.
positive_examples: The left side of 0=(0,...,0) is a vector, while each right-side entry is a scalar.
negative_examples: Interpreting x+0 as vector-plus-scalar addition when no such operation has been defined.
non_goals: This facet does not define a new operation between vectors and scalars.
error_signatures: Assuming every occurrence of 0 has the same mathematical type.
Ignoring the domain of vector addition.
instructional_repairs: Identify the type of every surrounding term before interpreting 0.
Choose the meaning that makes the defined operation well-typed.
